description:
We are a team of curious and ambitious problem-solvers passionate about science, engineering, technology, and space exploration.

Our interests lie at the intersection of robotics, artificial intelligence, electronics, automation, and scientific research. We enjoy exploring complex problems, learning new technologies, and developing unconventional solutions to real-world challenges.

We believe that great ideas emerge when different perspectives and areas of expertise come together
summary:
Up To Par is a free web tool that lets a farmer test a crop rotation on the past of their own field before risking a real season. In northern Kazakhstan wheat covers 75–87% of arable land and is traditionally rotated with summer fallow: one year in four the field earns nothing and lies bare, exposed to wind, and about 75% of the country’s farmland soils show some form of degradation.

Click any field on the map. The tool loads NASA POWER daily weather since 1981 and MODIS NDVI since 2000 directly from NASA, reads which years the field was fallow, and replays the farmer’s rotation and three alternatives without fallow through every real day using the FAO-56 soil-water method. In plain words and with the farmer’s own prices, it shows what fallow really gave the next crop, how often each rotation ran short of water, what it would have earned, how soil carbon changes, and what today’s NASA SMAP soil moisture suggests for next spring.
On eight fields across five regions, fallow gave the next wheat 28–49 mm more water at sowing, but the rotation harvested 7.5 years in 10 instead of 10. The model tracks NASA root-zone soil moisture (r = 0.75–0.95) and agrees with long-term field trials at Shortandy. The tool supports the farmer and the agronomist; it does not replace them
details:
What it does and how it works

Up To Par lets a grain farmer in northern Kazakhstan test a crop rotation on the past of their own field before changing anything in real life. The question it answers is the one farmers face every autumn: should this field go into fallow next year, or into a crop? Fallow is kept because it is believed to store water for the next wheat. Until now a farmer could not see how much water it really stored on their field, or what the same years would have looked like with peas, lentils, flax or oats instead.

The farmer picks one of eight prepared fields across five regions, or clicks any point on the map. The field opens full screen, as seen from orbit. Under the map is a timeline of every summer since 2000: ochre where the field lay bare, green where a crop grew. Press play and the map steps through the years. The farmer can switch between MODIS greenness, the MODIS photo of a given day, a sharp Sentinel-2 image, and today's soil moisture from NASA SMAP.

Below the map the page answers in six passes. It shows what the satellite saw on the field day by day, and compares the field with its neighbours in a 4 × 4 km window. It replays the current rotation and three alternatives without fallow through every real day of weather, and shows the money with the farmer's own prices. Then it shows what this autumn suggests for next spring, where the rain and snow went, and how soil carbon changes. A strategy card for each rotation says why it is offered, what the data show, what it gains, what is unknown and what to check with an agronomist.

Under the hood:

a) NASA POWER daily weather since 1981 drives an FAO-56 soil water balance for every day.

b) Yields respond to water stress through FAO-33 factors.

c) MODIS NDVI finds fallow years by thresholds. A k-means check on season curves agrees with them in 185 of 185 clear field-years.

d) Soil carbon is calibrated on long-term measurements at Shortandy.

e) The page reads NASA GIBS map tiles and turns pixel colours back into numbers. On our Kostanay field the decoded values matched the original MODIS values within 0.005.

f) Checks: the model's soil water tracks NASA POWER root-zone wetness (r = 0.75–0.95 on 1 May and 15 September), and the water gain from fallow falls within the range of the Shortandy rotation trial (Suleimenov et al., 2005).

Benefits

The farmer gets evidence from their own field, in plain words, in English or Russian, with their own prices. On our eight fields fallow gave the next wheat 28 to 49 mm more water at sowing. In exchange the field earns nothing for a year and stands bare. Rotations without fallow ran short of water more often, but harvested 10 years in 10 instead of 7.5 and gained soil carbon instead of losing it. The farmer sees both sides and decides. The tool is free, opens in any browser, and needs no login and no installation.

Intended impact

Wheat covers 75–87% of arable land in northern Kazakhstan, and about 75% of the country's farmland soils show some form of degradation. Fallow speeds up the loss of soil organic matter. Farmers rarely change a rotation on advice alone; a replay of their own field over 27 years is harder to dismiss. The same page also works for agronomists and extension services preparing advice for a district, and for any field in the world with local prices.

Tools

Python (standard library only) for data download and the reference model; JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the page; Leaflet for the map; Node.js for tests; GitHub Pages for hosting. The JavaScript model matches the Python model to 0.001 on 248 checks. There is no server and no special hardware: a laptop to build it, and any phone or computer with a browser to use it.

Creativity

The fallow audit is new. It does not tell the farmer what to grow. It shows what fallow actually did on their field, year by year, measured from orbit. Reading map colours back into numbers lets the page analyse any field on Earth in about a minute, with no server. When the main MODIS service went down during the hackathon, this method kept the tool working.

Next step: a community of farmers

A replay of the past is still a model. The strongest check of it is what farmers actually did on their fields. Our next step is a community inside Up To Para. A farmer shares a decision anonymously: for example, that they replaced fallow with peas, and what they harvested. Every report is checked against NASA MODIS: the page can see whether that field was really green that summer, so a made-up report stands out. Verified reports appear on the map next to neighbouring fields. A farmer then sees not only the model, but what people in the same district tried and what they got, and that persuades more than any chart. For us these reports become field data to test and calibrate the model. Yields and prices are commercial information, so a report shows only the district and the numbers, never the farm's name or exact location. A community needs a server and moderation, so we plan it after the hackathon. The current page stays free, with no login, and keeps working offline.

Other next steps

We will calibrate the soil humus model on Soviet-era and current agrochemical survey archives for the region, so the humus trend starts from measured values, not literature averages. We will cross-check NASA POWER rainfall with NASA GPM IMERG, which sees rain at a finer scale. We will replace the single-pixel point with real field boundaries. And we will bring the answer to farmers through a messenger bot, where many of them already discuss their fields.

What we took into account

Users. The users are farmers, not data scientists. Hence the plain language, a glossary, Russian next to English, and the farmer's own prices.

Uncertainty. Every number comes with its limits:

a) POWER weather describes the district, not the field.

b) SMAP covers a 9 km cell.

c) From orbit a fallow year and a crop failed by drought look the same.

What the model leaves out. Weeds, diseases and nitrogen are not modelled, so the strategy cards send those questions to a local agronomist.

Privacy. Data from the farmer's soil passport stays in their browser.

Respect for the farmer. The tool supports the decision; the farmer and the agronomist make it.
